title: Indications pour TP 01
text:
Here I give you some help in case you struggle solving the tasks. Please try to solve the tasks first without these hints, all information you need is in the .qmd document I shared with you.
Task 1
Use the R code chunk below and replace ____ with the name of the data frame (penguins). When you run the chunk, you will see the first rows:

head(____)







Show Hint





head() is a function. To use it, you put the name of the data set inside the parentheses. The name of the dataset is penguins, so you want to replace ____ with that name.



Learning Check 1
What does each row in penguins contain?

Data for all penguins at a specific island, e.g. Biscoe
Data for all penguins of a species, e.g. Adelie
Data for only one penguin







Show Hint





Try to imagine how the researchers entered the data. What would be the natural unit of observation for field biologists?



Task 2
Select the column bill_length_mm from the penguins data:

____$____







Show Hint





The name of the dataset is penguins, and you want to access a column called bill_length_mm. So first, you tell R the name of the data, then, that you want to access a column ($), and then you give the name of the column (bill_length_mm).



Task 3
Calculate the minimum, maximum, and mean value for bill_length_mm:

min(____$____)
max(____$____)
mean(____$____)







Show Hint





Above, you learned how to access a column in a data frame with the $ operator. Use the same method here, i.e. Insert in each function first the name of the data frame (penguins), then use $ to access the bill_length_mm column.



Task 4
Group the data by species and sex before calculating the mean of bill_length_mm:

penguins %>% # 1. Take the penguins dataset
  group_by(species, ____) %>% # 2. Group it by species and sex
  summarize(mean_bill_length_mm = mean(bill_length_mm)) # 3. create a new column called "mean_bill_length_mm" and assign the mean values of each group







Show Hint





group_by() works with multiple grouping variables. You can just add sex to group the data additionally by sex. The mean (step 3) will then be calculated for the combinations of both groups.



Task 5
Group the data by species and sex and additionally to the mean and minimum value of bill_length_mm, calculate the maximum value. Hint: If you create columns in R, they cannot contain spaces or minuses -.

penguins %>% # 1. Take the penguins dataset
  group_by(species, ____) %>% # 2. Group it by species and sex
  summarize(
    mean_bill_length_mm = mean(bill_length_mm), # 3.1. create a new column called "mean_bill_length_mm" and assign the mean values of each group
    min_bill_length_mm = min(bill_length_mm), # 3.2. create a new column called "min_bill_length_mm" and assign the minimum values of each group
    ____ = ____(____) # 3.3. create a new column called "max_bill_length_mm" and assign the maximum values of each group
  )







Show Hint





As in Task 4, group the data additionally by sex. In step 3.3, you can now calculate the maximum value of bill_length_mm. The name on the left of = is the name of the new column you will create. Call this column max_bill_length_mm. Remember, you create a new column before the =. Then use the max() function to calculate the maximum value of bill_length_mm.



Learning Check 2
Why do you think it is dangerous to do the following:

penguins <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie")







Show Hint





With the filter function you only retain a subset of the data. You would overwrite the entire dataset with only one species. Think about what would happen in later tasks.



Task 6
Create a new subset of the data. Use a reasonable name for the new data set. Filter to exclude Adelie penguins (with !=, see above), and a body_mass_g smaller or equal to 4000 g:

____ <- ____ %>%
  filter(____, ____)







Show Hint





First, select a reasonable name for the new subset of data you are creating. This name should reflect how you filtered the original data. penguins_chinstrap_entoo_light, peng_not_adelie_below4kg, etc. would work.
Next (after the <-), you have to give the data set you want to filter (penguins).
In the filter function, you want to first exclude all Adelie penguins. Think about this as “entries in column species is not equal to (!=) Adelie”. Remember that text in R needs to be wrapped with "".
As the second filtering step, only keep penguins below or equal to 4000 g. Think about this as “entries in column body_mass_g is smaller or equal to (<=) 4000 g”. Remember that numbers don’t need to be wrapped with "".
Remember that each condition inside filter() is separated by a comma.



Task 7
Use str() for the penguins data set:

str(____)







Show Hint





str() shows the structure of a data frame: variable types, lengths, etc. You have to insert the name of the data set (penguins) into the str() function.



Task 8
Use levels() below, to see the levels of penguins$island:

levels(____$____)







Show Hint





levels() shows all possible categories in a factor. This is useful before plotting or modelling categorical variables. You have to insert the name of the data set and of the column into the levels() function. Remember that you can access a column with the $ operator.

title: Indications pour TP 02
text:
Here I give you some help in case you struggle solving the tasks. Please try to solve the tasks first without these hints, all information you need is in the .qmd document I shared with you.
Task 1
Use different themes for the plot we created just above. Here is a list of standard themes but there are many R packages that extend your choice:

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  ____







Show Hint





Replace the ____ part with one of the themes in the list I gave you.



Task 2
Replace the ____ below with a colour scale of your choice.

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  ____







Show Hint





Replace the ____ part with one of the colour scale examples I gave you, e.g. scale_colour_colourblind().
If you want to use the “fully manual” colour scale, you could adapt it to something prettier like: scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "darkgreen","aquamarine2"))



Task 3
Take the plot we made above. Addditionally to different colours, use also different point shapes for the different species. Replace the ____ with the appropriate column name:

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, shape = ____)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





Think about how you want to plot the data. As you have already used the species column to define the colour of the data points, you can use it in a similar way to define the shape of the data points. Just replace ____ with species.



Task 4
So far, we used categorical data for the different colours. What happens if you use a numerical variable to define the different colours? Replace the ____ below with a numeric column, e.g. flipper_length_mm. Remember to also update the labels used for the colour. Chnage the ____ in labs() for something useful. Remember that any text needs to be wrapped with "".

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = ____, shape = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = ____) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





Above, you used the column spiecies for different colours, now, you are supposed to use the column flipper_length_mm. As a name for the legend (in labs()), you could use for example "Flipper length (mm)".



Task 5
Take a look at the plot you just made. What is the relationship between the bill length, body mass, and flipper length?







Show Hint





First, look only at the scatter plot. Try to understand how the values on one axis impact the values at the other axis. In the big picture, have penguins with a large bill length also a high body mass? Now, try to include the colour coded flipper length. Are there any patterns in the colours of the points that are related either to the x or y axis? More explicit, does the flipper lenght increase with the bill lenght and/or the body mass?



Task 6
You can change the width of the bars. This can be useful, because each bar represents the frequency of a range of values (e.g. 5 mm steps). You can do this with the bins argument. Try out different values below and see what happens:

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = ____) +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





What happens if you only use 1 or 2 bins? What happens if you use 100? 500? Replace the ____ with different values and see how the plot changes.



Task 7
Now plot in a similar way the island at which the penguins were observed. Use the island column.

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = ____)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count") +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





Again, think what you want to plot. You want to show a barplot with the frequency of islands on the y axis (calculated automatically) and the level of the island (e.g. Torgersen or Biscoe) on the x axis. Therefore, you have to give island as the x-axis.



Task 8
In this plot, the point represents the mean, and the line the standard deviation. Doing this for data grouped by island is not very useful. Adapt the plot below so that it shows the flipper length grouped by species:

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = ____, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_pointrange(stat = "summary", fun.data = mean_sdl) +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





Replace the ____ with species.



Task 9
What happens if you don’t use geom_jitter() but the “standard” geom_point()? Try it out below:

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  ____(alpha = .4) +
  geom_pointrange(stat = "summary", fun.data = mean_sdl) +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





You want to use a “normal” geom_point(). The second line will be: geom_point(alpha = .4) +.
Is the resulting plot useful? Why? How could it be improved?



Task 10
As a last step, try to customise the plot so that you archive something similar as this one. Think about which column is used for what.

Here is the “base” plot as a starting point:

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = .4) +
  geom_pointrange(stat = "summary", fun.data = mean_sdl) +
  theme_classic()







Show Hint





One possible solution is this:

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species),
) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = .75, shape = 21) +
  geom_pointrange(
    stat = "summary",
    fun.data = mean_sdl,
    show.legend = F,
    shape = 21
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  scale_fill_colorblind() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 20) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
